title: CASE OF MOLDOVAN AND OTHERS  v. ROMANIA (No. 1)
conclusion: Partly struck out of the list (friendly settlement);Severed and adjourned as regards seven applicants
summary:
In Moldovan and Others v. Romania (No. 1), the applicants were Romanian nationals of Roma origin from the village of Hădăreni, who brought a case against the Romanian state. The case centred on the extreme vulnerability of the Roma community following a violent outbreak in September 1993, when a dispute escalated into the killing of three Roma men and the destruction of Roma homes by a local mob, with the alleged involvement and encouragement of police officers. Over the course of one night, thirteen Roma houses were completely destroyed and several more badly damaged, forcing families to live for years in deplorable conditions such as animal shelters, cellars, and overcrowded, unheated rooms. Many applicants and their families suffered serious health consequences as a result.

Despite criminal and civil proceedings in Romania, the applicants faced inadequate investigations, lenient sentences for perpetrators, and insufficient compensation for their losses. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 6 (right to a fair trial), 8 (right to respect for private and family life), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The case was partly resolved through a friendly settlement, with the Romanian government agreeing to pay €262,000 in compensation and to implement measures to combat discrimination and improve conditions for Roma in Hădăreni.

This case is significant as it highlights the persistent challenges faced by Roma and Traveller communities in Europe, particularly regarding violence, discrimination, and state failure to protect their rights—a pattern rooted in a long history of marginalisation.
